s0003.literal: Hou Tian; Ouyang Wei, son He; Wu Mingche; Pei Zilie
s0003.idiomatic: Hou Tian; Ouyang Wei, son He; Wu Mingche; Pei Zilie

s0004.literal: Hou Tian, styled Boyu, was a native of Chongguo in Baxi.
s0004.idiomatic: Hou Tian, styled Boyu, came from Chongguo in Baxi.

s0005.literal: His father Hongyuan for generations had been a chieftain of western Shu.
s0005.idiomatic: His father Hongyuan's house had been chieftains in western Shu for generations.

s0006.literal: The Shu bandit Zhang Wene held White Cliff Mountain with troops numbering ten thousand; Liang Inspector of Yizhou the Prince of Poyang Xiao Fan ordered Hongyuan to campaign against him.
s0006.idiomatic: The Shu rebel Zhang Wene held White Cliff Mountain with ten thousand troops. Xiao Fan, Prince of Poyang and inspector of Yizhou, sent Hongyuan against him.

s0007.literal: Hongyuan died in battle; Tian firmly asked to take revenge, in every fight charging first into the breach, and at last beheaded Wene—by this he became known.
s0007.idiomatic: Hongyuan fell in battle. Tian begged to avenge him, led every charge himself, and at last struck off Wene's head—after that his name was known.

s0008.literal: Through serving Fan, Fan entrusted him with commanders' duties; whenever valley Yi and Liao in the mountains would not submit, he always sent Tian to campaign against them.
s0008.idiomatic: Serving Fan won his trust as a field commander; whenever mountain Yi and Liao would not submit, Fan sent Tian to bring them in.

s0009.literal: By accumulated merit he was made Central Army Major in the Light Chariots Office and Administrator of Jinkang.
s0009.idiomatic: Merit piled up until he was made central-army major in the Light Chariots Office and administrator of Jinkang.

s0010.literal: When Fan became Inspector of Yongzhou, Tian was made Supernal Martial General and Administrator of Fengyi.
s0010.idiomatic: When Fan became inspector of Yongzhou, Tian was made supernal-martial general and administrator of Fengyi.

s0011.literal: When Fan moved his garrison to Hefei, Tian again followed him.
s0011.idiomatic: When Fan shifted his garrison to Hefei, Tian went with him.

s0012.literal: When Hou Jing besieged the Terrace City, Fan then sent Tian to assist his heir Sih in relieving the capital.
s0012.idiomatic: When Hou Jing besieged the Terrace City, Fan sent Tian to help his heir Sih relieve the capital.

s0013.literal: When the capital fell, Tian and Sih withdrew to Hefei and still followed Fan in moving the garrison to Pencheng.
s0013.idiomatic: The capital fell. Tian and Sih fell back to Hefei and followed Fan when he moved the garrison to Pencheng.

s0014.literal: Before long both Fan and Sih died; Tian took over their troops and attached himself to Zhuang Tie, Administrator of Yuzhang.
s0014.idiomatic: Soon Fan and Sih both died. Tian took their troops and threw in with Zhuang Tie, administrator of Yuzhang.

s0015.literal: Tie suspected him; Tian feared and could not rest easy, pretended to summon Tie to discuss affairs, and thus killed him with a blade, seizing the territory of Yuzhang.
s0015.idiomatic: Tie mistrusted him. Tian, uneasy, lured Tie under pretense of counsel and killed him, seizing Yuzhang.

s0016.literal: Hou Jing's general Yu Qing when campaigning south reached Yuzhang; the cities all fell; Tian was hard pressed and then surrendered to Qing.
s0016.idiomatic: Hou Jing's general Yu Qing marched south to Yuzhang and took every town. Hard pressed, Tian surrendered to Qing.

s0017.literal: Qing sent Tian to Jing; Jing, because Tian bore the same surname, treated him as a clansman, received him very generously, and kept his wife, children, and younger brother as hostages.
s0017.idiomatic: Qing sent Tian to Jing. Jing claimed kinship by surname, treated him lavishly, and kept his wife, children, and younger brother as hostages.

s0018.literal: He sent Tian to follow Qing in pacifying the Li-man south of Lihu.
s0018.idiomatic: He sent Tian with Qing to pacify the Li country south of Lihu.

s0019.literal: When Jing was defeated at Baling, Jing's generals Song Zixian and Ren Yue were all captured by the Western armies; Tian then executed Jing's partisans to answer
s0019.idiomatic: When Jing was broken at Baling, his generals Song Zixian and Ren Yue were all taken by the loyal western armies. Tian executed Jing's partisans to join

s0021.literal: the Loyalist armies. Editorial footnote marker 1. Jing also executed Tian's younger brother and wife and children.
s0021.idiomatic: the loyalist armies. [1] Jing in turn put Tian's brother, wife, and children to death.

s0022.literal: Emperor Yuan of Liang appointed Tian Martial Retainer General, Inspector of South Yu, Marquis of Pixian, fief one thousand households.
s0022.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan of Liang made him martial-retainer general and inspector of South Yu, Marquis of Pixian, fief one thousand households.

s0023.literal: He still followed the commander-in-chief Wang Sengbian in campaigning against Jing, always as vanguard, in every battle gaining the advantage.
s0023.idiomatic: He still followed Wang Sengbian against Jing as vanguard and carried every fight.

s0024.literal: After the Terrace City was recovered, Jing fled to Wu commandery; Sengbian sent Tian to lead troops in pursuit; he fought Jing on the Wu Song River, utterly defeated Jing, and took all his military stores.
s0024.idiomatic: When the Terrace City was retaken Jing fled to Wu. Sengbian sent Tian in pursuit; on the Wu Song River he shattered Jing and seized all his stores.

s0025.literal: Advancing to Qiantang, Jing's generals Xie Daren, Lü Zirong, and others all surrendered.
s0025.idiomatic: He pressed on to Qiantang. Jing's generals Xie Daren, Lü Zirong, and the rest surrendered.

s0026.literal: For merit he was made Inspector of South Yu and garrisoned at Gushu.
s0026.idiomatic: For merit he was made inspector of South Yu and garrisoned Gushu.

s0027.literal: In the second year of Chengsheng, Qi sent Guo Yuanjian out from Ruxu; Sengbian sent Tian to lead three thousand armored men, build a fort at Dong Pass to resist him, and utterly defeated Yuanjian.
s0027.idiomatic: In Chengsheng year 2 Qi sent Guo Yuanjian from Ruxu. Sengbian sent Tian with three thousand armored men to fortify Dong Pass; he broke Yuanjian completely.

s0028.literal: He was made Bearer of the Staff, Pacifier of the North General, Editorial footnote marker 2. given one set of martial music, fief increased by two thousand households.
s0028.idiomatic: He received the staff as pacifier-of-the-north general [2], one suite of martial music, and two thousand more households in his fief.

s0029.literal: When Western Wei came to raid Jingzhou, Wang Sengbian made Tian vanguard to go to the rescue; he had not arrived when Jingzhou fell.
s0029.idiomatic: Western Wei raided Jingzhou. Sengbian made Tian vanguard of the relief force, but Jingzhou fell before he arrived.

s0030.literal: Tian went to Jiujiang and because of it escorted the Prince of Jin'an back to the capital.
s0030.idiomatic: Tian went to Jiujiang and escorted the Prince of Jin'an back to court.

s0031.literal: By imperial commission he was made Attendant-in-Ordinary, Bearer of the Staff, Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Jiang, Jin, Wu, and Qi, Inspector of Jiangzhou, enfeoffed Duke of Kangle county, fief five thousand households, advanced to Chariots-and-Cavalry General.
s0031.idiomatic: By regency commission he was attendant-in-ordinary, bearer of the staff, commander of Jiang, Jin, Wu, and Qi, inspector of Jiangzhou, Duke of Kangle, fief five thousand households, promoted to chariots-and-cavalry general.

s0032.literal: Minister of State Lu Fahe held Yingzhou and drew Qi troops to raid; Tian was then made commander of the army westward; before he arrived Fahe led his command north across the river into Qi.
s0032.idiomatic: Lu Fahe, minister of state, held Yingzhou and called in Qi. Tian was ordered west against him, but Fahe crossed north into Qi before he came up.

s0033.literal: Qi sent Murong Shide to garrison at Xiashou; Tian drew the western lines back and attacked by land and water; Shide's food ran out and he asked for peace; Tian returned to garrison Yuzhang.
s0033.idiomatic: Qi sent Murong Shide to Xiashou. Tian pulled the western front back and attacked by land and water until Shide's stores were gone and he sued for peace. Tian returned to Yuzhang.

s0034.literal: Sengbian sent his younger brother Sengyin with troops to join Tian in campaigning against Xiao Bo; when the Founder executed Sengbian, Sengyin secretly wished to plot against Tian and seize his army; Tian knew it, seized all Sengyin's partisans, and Sengyin fled to Qi.
s0034.idiomatic: Sengbian sent his brother Sengyin with troops to join Tian against Xiao Bo. When the Founder killed Sengbian, Sengyin meant to take Tian's army. Tian knew it, rounded up Sengyin's men, and Sengyin fled to Qi.

s0035.literal: In the second year of Shaotai, with his former title he was given the Grand Precedence of the Palace, all else as before.
s0035.idiomatic: In Shaotai year 2 he kept his rank and was given grand precedence of the palace; the rest unchanged.

s0036.literal: At that time Tian held the middle Yangzi and his troops were very strong; moreover he had long served Wang Sengbian; though outwardly he showed the forms of a subject, he had no mind to enter court.
s0036.idiomatic: Tian then held the middle river, his troops very strong, and he had served Sengbian long. He bowed in form but would not come to court.

s0037.literal: Earlier Yu Xiaoding had been Administrator of Yuzhang; when Tian garrisoned Yuzhang he then at Xinwu county separately built a walled stockade to resist Tian.
s0037.idiomatic: Yu Xiaoding had been administrator of Yuzhang. When Tian garrisoned there, Xiaoding built a separate walled camp at Xinwu to hold him off.

s0038.literal: Tian left the troops' wives and children at Yuzhang, ordered his cousin Shen to manage rear affairs, and sent all his troops to attack Xiaoding.
s0038.idiomatic: Tian left the troops' families at Yuzhang, put his cousin Shen in charge of the rear, and sent every soldier against Xiaoding.

s0039.literal: From summer to winter he could not take it; he then made a long siege and gathered in all the grain.
s0039.idiomatic: From summer through winter he could not break it. He settled into a long siege and stripped the fields bare.

s0040.literal: Shen was at odds with his subordinate Hou Fang'er; Editorial footnote marker 3. Fang'er in anger led his command to attack Shen, plundered the women, jewels, and gold of Tian's headquarters, and went over to the Founder.
s0040.idiomatic: Shen fell out with his man Hou Fang'er. [3] Fang'er in rage attacked Shen, looted Tian's headquarters of women, jewels, and gold, and went to the Founder.

s0041.literal: Tian having lost his base, the troops all scattered; he lightly returned to Yuzhang; the people of Yuzhang refused him; he then hurried to Pencheng and threw himself on his general Jiao Songdu.
s0041.idiomatic: Baseless, his troops broke. He slipped back to Yuzhang; the town shut him out. He ran to Pencheng and sought Jiao Songdu.

s0042.literal: Songdu urged Tian to go over to Qi; Tian thought the Founder was magnanimous and would surely spare him; he then came to the palace to beg pardon, and the Founder restored his rank and fief.
s0042.idiomatic: Songdu urged him toward Qi. Tian judged the Founder magnanimous and went to court to beg pardon. The Founder restored rank and fief.

s0043.literal: In the first year of Yongding he was made Attendant-in-Ordinary and Chariots-and-Cavalry General.
s0043.idiomatic: In Yongding year 1 he was made attendant-in-ordinary and chariots-and-cavalry general.

s0044.literal: In the second year he was advanced to Minister of Works.
s0044.idiomatic: In year 2 he rose to minister of works.

s0045.literal: When Wang Lin reached Dundu, Zhou Wenyü and Hou Andu were both drowned; Tian was then made Commander-in-Chief of the Western Campaign.
s0045.idiomatic: When Wang Lin reached Dundu, Zhou Wenyü and Hou Andu were both lost in the river. Tian was made commander of the western campaign.

s0047.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne he was further made Grand Commandant, fief increased by one thousand households.
s0047.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen took the throne Tian was made grand commandant with one thousand more households.

s0048.literal: When Wang Lin reached Zhakou, Tian was again made commander; Hou Andu and the others were all under his command.
s0048.idiomatic: When Lin reached Zhakou Tian was again commander; Hou Andu and the rest served under him.

s0049.literal: Tian and Lin faced each other for more than a hundred days without decision.
s0049.idiomatic: Tian and Lin locked for more than a hundred days without a decision.

s0050.literal: In the second month of the first year of Tiancheng, the spring waters at Dong Pass rose a little; ships could pass; Lin drew the troops of Chaohu at Hefei; war vessels followed one after another downriver; the momentum was very strong.
s0050.idiomatic: In Tiancheng year 1, second month, spring flood at Dong Pass let ships through. Lin brought Chaohu troops from Hefei downstream in a long line of war craft—the weight of it was immense.

s0051.literal: Tian led the army to advance to Beast-Barrier Isle; Editorial footnote marker 4. Lin also brought out ships and arrayed them on the west of the river, moored across the isle from them.
s0051.idiomatic: Tian advanced to Beast-Barrier Isle. [4] Lin ranged his fleet on the west bank across the isle.

s0052.literal: The next day they joined battle; Lin's army had little advantage and withdrew to hold the west bank.
s0052.idiomatic: They fought the next day. Lin gained little and pulled back to the west bank.

s0053.literal: By evening a northeast wind rose greatly and blew his ships; the ships were all wrecked, sunk in the sand; those drowned numbered in the tens and hundreds.
s0053.idiomatic: At dusk a northeast gale wrecked his fleet in the shallows. Tens and hundreds drowned.

s0054.literal: The waves were too great to return to the harbor; in the night a falling star also dropped into the rebel camp.
s0054.idiomatic: Waves blocked the harbor. That night a meteor fell in the rebel camp.

s0055.literal: When dawn came the wind was calm; Lin entered the harbor to repair ships, blocked the mouth with reed boats, and also ringed the shore with antlers; he did not dare come out again.
s0055.idiomatic: At dawn the wind fell. Lin crept into harbor, choked the mouth with reed boats, ringed the shore with antlers, and would not come out.

s0056.literal: At that time Western Wei sent the great general Shi Ning to press upriver; Tian heard it and knew Lin could not last, gathered the army and firmly held Lake Pu to wait for his exhaustion.
s0056.idiomatic: Western Wei sent Shi Ning upriver. Tian knew Lin could not hold, drew off, and camped on Lake Pu to wait him out.

s0057.literal: When Shi Ning arrived and besieged Yingzhou, Lin feared his troops would scatter; he then led the fleet downriver, moored ten li from Wuhu, and the night-watch sounded through the camp.
s0057.idiomatic: Shi Ning besieged Yingzhou. Lin, fearing collapse, came downstream and moored ten li from Wuhu; watches sounded all night.

s0058.literal: The next day Qi sent tens of thousands of troops to aid Lin; Lin led the troops toward Liangshan, wishing to pass the government army and hold a strategic point.
s0058.idiomatic: Next day Qi sent tens of thousands to help. Lin marched toward Liangshan to slip past the loyal army and seize a strong point.

s0059.literal: Qi's Yitong Liu Boqiu led more than ten thousand men to aid Lin in river fighting; Xingtai Murong Shide's son Zihui led two thousand iron cavalry on the south of Bowang Mountain on the west bank of Wuhu to lend him force.
s0059.idiomatic: Qi's Yitong Liu Boqiu brought ten thousand for the river fight. Murong Shide's son Zihui held two thousand horse on Bowang Mountain west of Wuhu as a screen.

s0060.literal: Tian ordered the army to cook at dawn and take bed-meals, divide mallets and sweep to halt at the tail of Wuhu Isle and wait for them.
s0060.idiomatic: Tian had the men cook at dawn, eat from their mats, and mass at the tail of Wuhu Isle.

s0061.literal: Editorial footnote marker 5. About to fight, a light breeze came from the southeast; the loyal army set rams and loosed fire.
s0061.idiomatic: [5] As battle neared, a light wind rose from the southeast. The loyal fleet set rams and fire.

s0062.literal: Dingzhou Inspector Zhang Zhaoda rode the Level-Barbarians great ship straight up the mid-river, launched rams and struck the rebel ships; the rest—assault craft and Green Dragons—each took their match.
s0062.idiomatic: Zhang Zhaoda of Dingzhou drove the Level-Barbarians in midstream, smashed rebel hulls with rams; assault craft and Green Dragons paired off ship for ship.

s0063.literal: They also covered rush boats in oxhide, used them to strike rebel ships, and also poured molten iron.
s0063.idiomatic: Oxhide-sheathed rush boats rammed the rebels; molten iron rained down.

s0065.literal: His infantry on the west bank trampled one another; horsemen were all mired in the reeds; only one or two in ten of tethered horses broke loose and escaped.
s0065.idiomatic: Infantry on the west bank trampled each other. Horse sank in the reeds; only one or two in ten broke their tethers and fled.

s0066.literal: They took all his ships and gear, captured alive the Qi generals Liu Boqiu and Murong Zihui; the rest of prisoners and heads numbered in the tens of thousands.
s0066.idiomatic: They seized every ship and weapon, took Liu Boqiu and Murong Zihui alive, and counted prisoners and heads by the ten thousand.

s0067.literal: Lin with his partisans Pan Chunnian and others took a single skiff and burst through the line to flee to Pencheng; he still wished to gather the scattered; no troops would follow; he then with wife, concubines, and a dozen attendants entered Qi.
s0067.idiomatic: Lin, Pan Chunnian, and a few others broke out in one skiff to Pencheng, tried to rally the broken, found no troops would follow, and crossed to Qi with wife, concubines, and a dozen attendants.

s0069.literal: That year an edict made Tian Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Xiang, Ba, Ying, Jiang, Wu, and the other five provinces, garrisoning Pencheng.
s0069.idiomatic: That year he was ordered commander of Xiang, Ba, Ying, Jiang, Wu, and four other provinces, garrisoning Pencheng.

s0070.literal: When Zhou generals He Ruo Dun and Dugu Sheng raided Ba and Xiang, Tian was again made commander of the western campaign; he fought Sheng at West River Mouth, utterly defeated Sheng's army, and captured men, horses, and gear beyond counting.
s0070.idiomatic: Zhou's He Ruo Dun and Dugu Sheng raided Ba and Xiang. Tian was western commander again, broke Sheng at West River Mouth, and took men, horses, and gear past counting.

s0071.literal: For merit he was made Bearer of the Staff, Commander-in-Chief of Xiang, Gui, Ying, Ba, Wu, and Yuan, Inspector of Xiangzhou, enfeoffed Duke of Lingling commandery, fief seven thousand households, the rest as before.
s0071.idiomatic: For merit he received the staff, command of six provinces, inspectorship of Xiangzhou, dukedom of Lingling, fief seven thousand households; the rest unchanged.

s0072.literal: In the second year, because of illness he memorialized asking to return to court.
s0072.idiomatic: In year 2 illness drove him to ask leave for the capital.

s0073.literal: In the third month he died on the road, aged fifty-two.
s0073.idiomatic: He died on the road in the third month, aged fifty-two.

s0074.literal: He was posthumously made Attendant-in-Ordinary, Rapid Cavalry General, Grand Marshal, with feather canopy, martial music, twenty sword-guards in the procession, Eastern Garden secret rites, posthumous title Zhuangsu.
s0074.idiomatic: Posthumously he was attendant-in-ordinary, rapid-cavalry general, grand marshal, with feather canopy, martial music, twenty sword-guards, Eastern Garden rites, posthumous name Zhuangsu.

s0075.literal: In the ninth month of that year he was given place in the Founder's temple hall.
s0075.idiomatic: That ninth month he entered the Founder's temple.

s0077.literal: Jingzang married Emperor Wen's second daughter the Princess of Fuyang; because of the princess he was made Extraordinary Cadet of the Dispersed Cavalry.
s0077.idiomatic: Jingzang married Emperor Wen's second daughter, the Princess of Fuyang, and by that match was made extraordinary cadet of the dispersed cavalry.

s0078.literal: In the third year of Taijian he died; posthumously made Registrar of the Minister of State.
s0078.idiomatic: He died in Taijian year 3 and was posthumously registrar to the minister of state.

s0079.literal: Jingzang had no son; his younger brother Jiu inherited the fief.
s0079.idiomatic: Jingzang had no son; his brother Jiu inherited the fief.

s0080.literal: Ouyang Wei, styled Jingshi, was a native of Linxiang in Changsha.
s0080.idiomatic: Ouyang Wei, styled Jingshi, came from Linxiang in Changsha.

s0081.literal: He was a great clan of the commandery.
s0081.idiomatic: His house was a great clan of the commandery.

s0082.literal: His grandfather Jingda in the Liang generation was Administrator of the commandery.
s0082.idiomatic: His grandfather Jingda had been the commandery administrator under Liang.

s0083.literal: His father Sengbao was Commandant of Escort Cavalry.
s0083.idiomatic: His father Sengbao was commandant of escort cavalry.

s0084.literal: Wei in youth was plain and upright and had powers of thought; by conduct and speech of deep trust he was known beyond the mountain passes.
s0084.idiomatic: In youth he was plain, upright, and thoughtful; south of the passes he was known for trustworthy conduct.

s0085.literal: At his father's death he was wasted by grief to the utmost.
s0085.idiomatic: His father's death wasted him with grief.

s0086.literal: The family's accumulated wealth he entirely yielded to his elder brothers.
s0086.idiomatic: He gave the family's accumulated wealth entirely to his elder brothers.

s0087.literal: The province and commandery repeatedly summoned him but he would not respond; he then built a hut beside Lushan Temple, devoted himself to study, and broadly mastered the classics and histories.
s0087.idiomatic: Province and commandery summoned him in vain. He built a hut by Lushan Temple, studied hard, and mastered classics and histories.

s0088.literal: At thirty his elder brother forced him to enter office; he began as Central Army Major in the Trustworthy Martial Office and was transferred to Central Army Major on the staff of the Prince of Shaoling, General Who Pacifies the West.
s0088.idiomatic: At thirty his brother forced him into service: central-army major in the Trustworthy Martial Office, then on the staff of the Prince of Shaoling, general who pacifies the west.

s0089.literal: Liang's Left Rapid General Lan Qin in his youth was friendly with Wei; therefore Wei often followed Qin on campaigns.
s0089.idiomatic: In youth he was close to Liang's left-rapid general Lan Qin and often campaigned with him.

s0090.literal: When Qin was made Inspector of Hengzhou, Wei was still made Administrator of Qingyuan.
s0090.idiomatic: When Qin became inspector of Hengzhou, Wei was made administrator of Qingyuan.

s0091.literal: Qin campaigned south against the Yi and Liao, captured Chen Wenche; the booty could not be counted; he presented a great bronze drum such as no generation had had; Wei shared in the merit.
s0091.idiomatic: Qin marched south against Yi and Liao, took Chen Wenche, and seized booty past counting, including a great bronze drum none had seen. Wei shared the credit.

s0092.literal: Returning he was made Direct Attendant General and still made Administrator of Tianmen; campaigning against the southern Man he had merit.
s0092.idiomatic: Back at court he was direct-attendant general and administrator of Tianmen; against the southern Man he won merit.

s0093.literal: Inspector the Prince of Luling Xiao Xu deeply praised him and took him as a client.
s0093.idiomatic: The Prince of Luling, inspector Xiao Xu, prized him and took him as client.

s0094.literal: When Qin campaigned against Jiaozhou he again asked Wei to go with him.
s0094.idiomatic: When Qin marched on Jiaozhi he asked Wei along again.

s0095.literal: Qin crossed the mountains and died of illness; Wei was made Interior Minister of Linhe; he memorialized asking to send Qin's coffin back to the capital and only then take up his post.
s0095.idiomatic: Qin died crossing the ridge. Wei was made interior minister of Linhe, begged to send the coffin home first, then take office.

s0096.literal: At that time more than fifty caves on the border of Xiang and Heng would not submit; the order still went to Inspector of Hengzhou Wei Can to campaign against them; Can entrusted Wei as commander and all were pacified and destroyed.
s0096.idiomatic: More than fifty caves between Xiang and Heng would not submit. Wei Can, inspector of Hengzhou, put Wei in command and wiped them out.

s0097.literal: Can memorialized to Liang Wu, praising Wei's sincerity and ability; an edict came down with rewards; he was still made Supernal Martial General to campaign against the mountain bandits of Guang and Heng.
s0097.idiomatic: Can praised his loyalty and skill to Emperor Wu of Liang. Rewards came down; he was made supernal-martial general against the mountain bandits of Guang and Heng.

s0098.literal: When Hou Jing hatched rebellion, Can removed himself and returned to the capital to campaign against Jing; he left Wei to oversee Hengzhou.
s0098.idiomatic: When Hou Jing rebelled, Can went back to fight him and left Wei to oversee Hengzhou.

s0099.literal: After the capital fell, south of the mountains they devoured one another; Lan Qin's younger brother the former Inspector of Gaozhou Yu attacked the Interior Minister of Shixing Xiao Shaoji; Editorial footnote marker 7. and seized his commandery.
s0099.idiomatic: After the capital fell the south tore itself apart. Qin's brother Yu, former inspector of Gaozhou, attacked Shixing interior minister Xiao Shaoji [7] and seized his commandery.

s0100.literal: Yu, because his elder brother Qin and Wei were old friends, sent to recruit him; Wei would not follow.
s0100.idiomatic: Yu, remembering Qin's friendship with Wei, sent to recruit him. Wei refused.
